This pattern raises concern for several conditions — notably erythema multiforme (often with “target lesions” and mucosal involvement), contact dermatitis (but perioral sparing is atypical), or more urgently, measles (classically starts on face, spares perioral region, then descends; often with prodrome). Perioral sparing is a well-recognized feature of measles exanthem. The absence of new medications makes drug eruption less likely. While other viral exanthems (e.g., parvovirus B19) can cause facial rash, they typically lack perioral sparing and don’t follow this exact descending pattern. Koplik spots (small, bluish-white papules on erythematous buccal mucosa) are pathognomonic for measles and typically appear 1–2 days before the rash.
